title: Unit – 5 : Session – 8 : SLO – 1  |  Shortest Path — Dijkstra's Algorithm
sections: I. Fill in the Blanks
Dijkstra's algorithm is used to find the SHORTEST path from a source vertex to all other vertices.
Dijkstra's algorithm cannot handle graphs with NEGATIVE edge weights.
The primary data structure used to track minimum distances is a PRIORITY QUEUE (min-heap).
The time complexity of Dijkstra's using a priority queue (min-heap) is O((V + E) log V).
Dijkstra's algorithm is a type of GREEDY algorithm.
II. True or False
Dijkstra's algorithm is applicable to both directed and undirected graphs — TRUE.
Dijkstra's algorithm can be used for negative weight edges — FALSE.
The shortest path from source to destination always forms a tree structure — TRUE (shortest-path tree).
Dijkstra's algorithm always visits the closest unvisited vertex next — TRUE.
III. Reasoning Questions
Negative weights: Dijkstra's finalizes a vertex's distance when it is visited; a later negative edge could
improve an already-finalized distance, breaking the greedy assumption. (Use Bellman-Ford instead.)
Difference from Prim's: Prim's computes a MINIMUM SPANNING TREE (minimum total edge weight connecting all
vertices); Dijkstra's computes SHORTEST PATH distances from one source to all vertices.
Real-life application: GPS / Google Maps route finding (road network with travel-time weights); also
network routing protocols (OSPF).
IV. Match the Following
1. Dijkstra's Algorithm — d) Cannot handle negative weight edges
2. Priority Queue — f) Data structure to pick minimum value
3. Source vertex distance — e) Initialized to 0
4. Graph with negative edge weight — d) (cannot be handled by Dijkstra's; needs Bellman-Ford)
5. Kruskal's Algorithm — c) Computes Minimum Spanning Tree
6. Dijkstra vs Prim's — a) One for shortest path, one for MST
